name: Broomfield House
text: Your train passes near Broomfield House, on the train's {side}, in Broomfield Park. Bought by the London merchant Joseph Jackson in 1624, it was damaged by fires in 1984, 1993, 1994 and 2019, and plans to restore it had made no progress by January 2024.

name: Intimate Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Intimate Theatre, on the train's {side}, the name long used for St Monica's church hall on Green Lanes. The actor John Clements made it a theatre in 1935; Roger Moore later acted in its repertory company, and David Bowie appeared on its stage in 1968.

name: Grange Park Methodist Church
text: Your train passes near Grange Park Methodist Church, on the train's {side}, also known as the Church in the Orchard. Designed by Charles H. Brightiff in the Art Deco style, it opened in 1938.

name: Trinity Church, Enfield
text: Your train passes near Trinity Church, Enfield, on the train's {side}, a ragstone church with a tall spire, built for the Methodists in 1889. Badly damaged by fire in 1919, it reopened the next year; in the Second World War its basement was an air raid precautions control centre.

name: St Michael and All Angels, Enfield
text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels church, on the train's {side}, begun in 1873. A year later the money ran out, and the unfinished west end was closed off with a temporary wall that was not replaced until 1963.

name: Lavender Hill Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Lavender Hill Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1872 with two facing Gothic chapels, one for Anglicans and one for nonconformists. Its gates were “Cemetery Gates”, the end of Stan and Jack's bus route in the sitcom On the Buses.

name: New Beacon Books
text: Your train passes near New Beacon Books, on the train's {side}, founded in 1966 by John La Rose and Sarah White as the first Caribbean publishing house in England. Its bookshop has been at 76 Stroud Green Road since 1973, with the George Padmore Institute on the floors above.

name: Emirates Stadium
text: Your train passes near the Emirates Stadium, on the train's {side}, Arsenal's home since 2006. The club built it on an industrial and waste site at Ashburton Grove after being refused permission to enlarge Highbury; it seats more than 60,000.

name: Islington Central Library
text: Your train passes near Islington Central Library, on the train's {side}, opened in 1907 as the largest municipal library in London, partly paid for by Andrew Carnegie. Its architect, Henry T. Hare, was known for putting a hare somewhere in his designs.

name: HM Prison Pentonville
text: Your train passes near HM Prison Pentonville, on the train's {side}, opened in 1842 with four wings radiating from a central hall, so that staff could see along them all. It became the model for British prisons: 54 more were built to similar designs within six years.

name: Canonbury Tower
text: Your train passes near Canonbury Tower, on the train's {side}, the oldest building in Islington: the main surviving part of a manor house built for the canons of St Bartholomew's Priory between 1509 and 1532. Thomas Cromwell, Francis Bacon and Oliver Goldsmith were among its owners or occupants.

name: Union Chapel
text: Your train passes near Union Chapel, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed Gothic Revival church of the late 19th century that is still a working Congregational church. It is also a music venue known for its acoustics, and a drop-in centre for people facing homelessness.

name: Bunhill Fields
text: Your train passes near Bunhill Fields, on the train's {side}, a burial ground from 1665 to 1854 that took about 123,000 burials. John Bunyan, Daniel Defoe and William Blake are among those buried there; most of it is now a public garden.

name: John Wesley's House
text: Your train passes near John Wesley's House, on the train's {side}, built in 1779 beside Wesley's Chapel on City Road. John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, lived there for the last 12 years of his life and died in his bedroom.

name: London Charterhouse
text: Your train passes near the London Charterhouse, on the train's {side}, founded as a Carthusian priory in 1371 on the site of a Black Death burial ground. Thomas Sutton bought it in 1611 for a school and an almshouse; the almshouse is still lived in, while the school moved to Godalming in 1872.

name: Sir John Soane's Museum
text: Your train passes near Sir John Soane's Museum, on the train's {side}, the architect's own house, full of his drawings, models, paintings and antiquities. An Act of Parliament of 1833 left it to the nation, to be kept as nearly as possible as he left it, partly so that he could disinherit a son he disliked.

name: 25 Brook Street
text: Your train passes near 25 Brook Street, on the train's {side}, where the composer George Frideric Handel lived from 1723 until his death in 1759 and wrote almost all his later works. Jimi Hendrix lived next door at number 23; the two houses are now the museum Handel Hendrix House.

name: Marble Arch
text: Your train passes near Marble Arch, on the train's {side}, designed by John Nash in 1827 as the state entrance to the courtyard of Buckingham Palace. It was moved here, near the corner of Hyde Park, in 1851, when Queen Victoria enlarged the palace.

name: Christ Church Spitalfields
text: Your train passes near Christ Church Spitalfields, on the train's {side}, built between 1714 and 1729 to Nicholas Hawksmoor's design. It was one of the first churches of the commission set up in 1711 to build 50 new churches for London's new districts.

name: The Theatre
text: Your train passes near the site of The Theatre, on the train's {side}, built by James Burbage in 1576 as the first permanent theatre in England made only for plays. Shakespeare's company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, played there; after a dispute with the landlord its timbers went to build the Globe on Bankside.

name: Museum of the Home
text: Your train passes near the Museum of the Home, on the train's {side}, formerly the Geffrye Museum, in almshouses built in 1714 for the widows of ironmongers with money left by Sir Robert Geffrye, a Lord Mayor of London. It explores home life from 1600 to the present day.

name: Hoxton Hall
text: Your train passes near Hoxton Hall, on the train's {side}, built as MacDonald's Music Hall in 1863. It lost its licence in 1871 after complaints by the police, and was later a Quaker meeting house for many years, which is why its galleried auditorium survives largely as it was built.

name: Clowns Gallery and Archives
text: Your train passes near the Clowns Gallery and Archives, on the train's {side}, set up in 1959 in the vestry of Holy Trinity Church, Dalston, and closed since 2018. It keeps the Clown Egg Register: since 1946, clowns' face designs have been painted on eggs so that no two clowns share a face.

name: Vortex Jazz Club
text: Your train passes near the Vortex Jazz Club, on the train's {side}, founded by David Mossman in 1988 in Stoke Newington Church Street. It moved to Gillett Square in Dalston in 2005, and the square opened the next year with a performance by 200 saxophonists.

name: St Augustine's Tower
text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Tower, on the train's {side}, all that is left of Hackney's early 16th-century parish church. A working 16th-century turret clock has been inside since at least 1608, and the tower appears on the London Borough of Hackney's coat of arms.

name: Rio Cinema
text: Your train passes near the Rio Cinema, on the train's {side}, which opened as the Kingsland Palace in 1909 and was rebuilt as the Kingsland Empire in 1915. F. E. Bromige gave it its Art Deco look in 1937; it was renamed the Rio in 1976, and from 1979 local people ran it as a community cooperative.

name: Sutton House
text: Your train passes near Sutton House, on the train's {side}, built in 1535 by Sir Ralph Sadler, Henry VIII's Principal Secretary of State. The oldest home in Hackney, it is a rare red-brick Tudor house and belongs to the National Trust.

name: V&A East
text: Your train passes near V&A East, on the train's {side}, the Victoria and Albert Museum's outpost in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. Its storehouse opened in May 2025 and its museum on April 18th 2026, the V&A's sixth site.

name: St Mary of Eton
text: Your train passes near St Mary of Eton church, on the train's {side}, built in 1890 to 1892 for a mission that Eton College set up in Hackney Wick, to help local people and show its pupils how they lived. The 59 Club, a Church of England youth club, was founded there.

name: London Aquatics Centre
text: Your train passes near the London Aquatics Centre, on the train's {side}, designed by Zaha Hadid for the swimming and diving at the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Under its wave-like roof are two swimming pools and a diving pool; it opened to the public in 2014.

name: ArcelorMittal Orbit
text: Your train passes near the ArcelorMittal Orbit, on the train's {side}, a 114.5-metre sculpture and observation tower by Anish Kapoor and Cecil Balmond, built for the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. It is Britain's largest piece of public art; in 2016 a slide, then the world's longest, was added.

name: All Hallows-on-the-Wall
text: Your train passes near All Hallows-on-the-Wall, on the train's {side}, a church beside the line of London's old city wall. The present building was designed by George Dance the Younger in 1767, when he was only 24; the church before it was known for the hermits who lived in cells there.

name: Young V&A
text: Your train passes near the Young V&A, on the train's {side}, the V&A's museum for children, opened in 1872 as the Bethnal Green Museum. Its iron frame was first put up in South Kensington in 1856 to 1857; the museum won Museum of the Year in 2024.

name: Keeling House
text: Your train passes near Keeling House, on the train's {side}, a 16-storey block designed by Denys Lasdun and finished in 1957. He grouped four blocks of maisonettes round a central tower, hoping to keep the neighbourliness of Victorian terraced streets; it was renovated in 2001 with a new penthouse floor.

name: Hackney Empire
text: Your train passes near the Hackney Empire, on the train's {side}, designed by Frank Matcham and built in 1901 as a music hall. Charlie Chaplin, Stan Laurel, Marie Lloyd and Gracie Fields all performed there.

name: Mossbourne Community Academy
text: Your train passes near Mossbourne Community Academy, on the train's {side}, opened in 2004 on the site of Hackney Downs School. Sir Clive Bourne founded it as one of England's first city academies, and its buildings were designed by Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners.

name: Gibson Gardens
text: Your train passes near Gibson Gardens, on the train's {side}, tenement flats built in 1880 by the Metropolitan Association for Improving the Dwellings of the Industrious Classes. They were some of the first good-quality homes in London for working and lower-middle-class families.

name: Abney Park Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Abney Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, one of London's “Magnificent Seven” cemeteries, opened in 1840 as a non-denominational garden cemetery and arboretum. Nearly 197,000 burials had taken place there by 2000; it is now a local nature reserve.

name: St Ignatius Church, Stamford Hill
text: Your train passes near St Ignatius Church, on the train's {side}, a large Roman Catholic church run by the Jesuits. Cardinal Herbert Vaughan invited them to found the parish, which they did in 1894, after nearly 300 local people had asked for one.

name: Marcus Garvey Library
text: Your train passes near the Marcus Garvey Library, on the train's {side}, opened in 1987 and named after the activist Marcus Garvey, whose son, Marcus Garvey III, laid its foundation stone. Its Black Literature and Marcus Garvey collections are used by the local Black community.
